To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the sieving equation derived by Landis and Pappenheimer for calculating the sieving coefficient of solutes of different sizes has to be modified to include the effect of convection; and (2) the mean effective glmerular pressure can be calculated from the mean sieved curve obtained from a series of experiments.
a new model for the calculation of the sieving coefficients of biological membranes has been developed and tested.

the permeability of the glomerular capillary wall can be measured by determining the sieving coefficients of a series of solute fractions of increasing size, and that the permeability can be described as a function of the mean effective pressure.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new methods to measure the glomerular permeability.
the application of the transport equation describing the passage of a solute through a membrane to the glomerulus.
the application of the transport theory of solute flow across membranes to the glomerulus.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the sieving curves of [125I]PVP in normal dog kidneys can be explained by the presence of a single population of cylindrical pores of 19.5 ± 0.5 Å in radius and a total area per unit of length of the pores of 0.5 × 10−5 cm2/cm.

the glomerular sieved PVP molecules move through the membrane by a combination of diffusion and convective flow, and the sieving coefficients are not only dependent on the molecular size of the solutes.
the glomerular filtration barrier is a porous system with pores of a mean radius of 19.6 Å, a total pore area of 0.0005 cm2/cm, and an effective filtration pressure of 15.6 mm Hg.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the sieving coefficient of a substance is determined by the size of its molecule and by the size of the pore.
the glomerular filtration is not an ultrafiltration process, but a filtration process in which the convective transport of solutes is important.
a better understanding of the transport mechanisms through the glomerular membrane has been obtained, which may be applied to other biological membranes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the sieving equation derived from the transport equation is more appropriate than the classical sieving equation for the calculation of the glomerular sievability.
the transport of solute molecules across the glomerular capillary wall is a complex process involving both diffusion and convection, which can only be described by a combination of the two processes.
a more accurate sieving curve can be obtained by using the new equations.
